lessons.title: Introduction to Bash
lessons.content:
Bash (Bourne Again Shell) is a command programming language interpreter, that executes commands read from the standard input or from a file. It's the default shell on most Linux distributions and macOS. The shell is the program that reads and executes commands via the command line that affects your entire machine.

Bash Scripting is a scripting language, which means that it was specically designed to automate tasks for system admins, software engineers, IT, and Cyber Security on Linux machines. In addition, since Bash scripts have the ability to modify system files, hackers use Bash scripts to perform attacks which could allow them to compromise your system. Overall, learning Bash Scripting could open the door for better career oppurtunites, enhance your programming skills, and give you a better understaning of Linux.
tips: WARNING: This section of Linux-Lab assumes you already know a programming language (Preferably in Python, C, or C++). If not then prepare for a fast paced enviroment as this section will use concepts that will make more sense for an experienced programmer.

lessons.title: Hello World
lessons.content:
Every Bash script begins with the shebang character sequence: #!. Followed by the absolute path that the interpreter uses to execute the script: #!/bin/bash.

To print to the screen, we follow the same command used in the Linux command line: echo. The difference is that echo can now take different parameters like strings, chars, ints, arrays, and more.

For the first lesson here, lets print to the screen: "Hello World".
tips: Make sure your script file has executable permissions: use `chmod +x script.sh`. In this enviorement you wont need to, but if you are programming on your own machine, you will need to allow user execution permissions.
Use double quotes (`"`) around strings to preserve spaces and interpret variables correctly.

lessons.title: $Variables
lessons.content:
Since Bash is a scripting language, variables are not type-strict. You don't declare them with a data type — you simply assign them using the equals sign (`=`), and reference them using the dollar sign (`$`). Bash is not type-strict, everything is stored as a string by default. It's only interpreted as a number when used in an arithmetic context.

Let's write a program that demonstrates how you can create and reference variables in Bash:

food="Pizza"
echo "I like, $food"

Note: The Bash interperter knows that food is a string variable because it is not used in an arthmethic context (we wil discuss about this in the next lesson). The variable (whether it is a string, int, char, etc) is extracted or referenced in the echo paramater, in this case the variable food represents a string. Also, there should be no spaces around the equals sign when assigning a value. In addition, double quotes are recommended to preserve spacing and interpret variable values properly.
tips: Variable assignment must not have spaces around the `=`. For example: `x=5`, not `x = 5`.
All variables are treated as strings by default unless used in arithmetic expressions.
Variable names should start with a letter or underscore, not a number.
